subtopics.name: Aging process and older adult health

questions.stem: A client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea is on contact precautions. After emptying the client's bedpan and removing gloves and gown, the nurse prepares to leave the room. How should the nurse clean their hands?

options.text: Rub the hands with an alcohol-based hand sanitizer for at least 20 seconds
Wash the hands with soap and water, using friction for at least 20 seconds
Apply hand sanitizer, then put on a new pair of gloves before touching anything else
Rinse the hands under running water without soap, then dry them with a paper towel

rationale.correct: Spore-forming organisms such as C. difficile need handwashing with soap and water; alcohol-based rubs do not kill spores.

perOption.a: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores, so hand rub alone is not enough after this contact.
perOption.b: Soap, water and friction physically remove C. difficile spores, which alcohol rubs do not destroy.
perOption.c: Gloves over contaminated hands do not remove spores.
perOption.d: Water alone does not remove spores; soap and friction are needed.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose hand hygiene for C. difficile.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting several clients. For each condition, indicate the transmission-based precautions the nurse should start.

rows.text: A draining wound infected with MRSA
Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis with a productive cough

rationale.correct: Airborne: measles, TB, varicella. Droplet: influenza, pertussis, meningococcus. Contact: MRSA, C. difficile, scabies.

perOption.r1:c1: Measles spreads by tiny airborne particles; it needs a negative-pressure room and an N95 respirator.
perOption.r1:c2: Droplet precautions do not protect against measles, which stays suspended in air.
perOption.r1:c3: Contact precautions alone do not stop airborne spread.
perOption.r2:c1: Pertussis is spread by large droplets, not airborne particles.
perOption.r2:c2: Pertussis spreads by large droplets within about 2 m; a surgical mask is worn.
perOption.r2:c3: Contact precautions alone miss the droplet route.
perOption.r3:c1: MRSA in a wound does not spread through the air.
perOption.r3:c2: Droplet precautions are used for respiratory spread, not a wound.
perOption.r3:c3: MRSA spreads by direct and indirect contact; gown and gloves are needed.
perOption.r4:c1: TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei; it needs an airborne infection isolation room and an N95.
perOption.r4:c2: A surgical mask for staff does not filter TB particles.
perOption.r4:c3: Contact precautions do not address airborne spread.
perOption.r5:c1: Influenza is managed with droplet precautions in routine care.
perOption.r5:c2: Influenza spreads by large respiratory droplets.
perOption.r5:c3: Contact alone misses the main droplet route.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions while wearing gloves, a gown, a surgical mask and goggles. Place the steps for removing personal protective equipment in the order the CDC recommends.

rationale.correct: Doffing order: gloves, goggles or face shield, gown, mask or respirator, then hand hygiene.

perOption.a: Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off first.
perOption.b: Eye protection is removed by the earpieces after the gloves.
perOption.c: The gown is pulled away from the body, turning it inside out.
perOption.d: The mask is removed last, by the ties or ear loops.
perOption.e: Hands are cleaned right after all PPE is removed.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.educationalObjective: Remove PPE in the correct order.

questions.stem: The nurse is assisting with placement of a central venous catheter at the bedside. The provider's sterile gloved hand brushes against the unsterile bed rail while reaching for a guidewire. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the provider that the glove touched the rail and offer a new pair of sterile gloves
Wipe the glove with an alcohol pad so the procedure can continue without a delay
Wait until the procedure ends, then report the breach through an incident report
Watch the insertion site closely for redness or drainage over the next 48 hours

rationale.correct: Anyone who sees a break in sterile technique must speak up right away so it can be corrected before harm occurs.

perOption.a: A sterile glove that touches an unsterile surface is contaminated; the nurse speaks up so it can be changed before the line is placed.
perOption.b: Alcohol does not make a contaminated glove sterile again.
perOption.c: Waiting allows a contaminated glove to touch the catheter, which raises the risk of a bloodstream infection.
perOption.d: Monitoring does not prevent infection from a known break in sterile technique.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a break in sterile technique.

questions.stem: While hanging an IV bag of cyclophosphamide, the nurse notices about 15 mL of the drug has leaked onto the floor beside the client's chair. After asking the client to stay seated, what should the nurse do next?

options.text: Wipe up the spill with paper towels and put them in a red biohazard bag
Get the hazardous drug spill kit and put on its gown, double gloves and eye protection
Call environmental services to clean the spill and continue the infusion
Pour a disinfectant solution on the spill and leave it to dry for 10 minutes

rationale.correct: Hazardous drug spills are contained right away using a spill kit and full PPE, cleaned from the outside in, and disposed of as hazardous waste.

perOption.a: Chemotherapy waste goes in a hazardous drug container, and the spill kit's protective equipment is needed first.
perOption.b: Cleanup starts with protecting the nurse using the spill kit, then containing the spill from the outside in.
perOption.c: The spill should be contained right away by trained staff with a spill kit; leaving it spreads contamination.
perOption.d: Disinfectants do not neutralize most chemotherapy drugs and can spread the spill.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is admitted with varicella (chickenpox). The child's lesions appeared 2 days ago, and new ones are still forming. Which staff assignment is safest?

options.text: A nurse who had chickenpox as a child and is now 12 weeks pregnant
A nurse who received two doses of varicella vaccine and has documented immunity
A nurse who is taking oral prednisone 40 mg daily for an asthma flare
A nurse whose immunity is unknown but who will wear an N95 respirator in the room

rationale.correct: Assign staff with documented immunity to clients with varicella, and protect staff who are pregnant or immunosuppressed.

perOption.a: Immunity from past disease protects the nurse, but varicella exposure in pregnancy is usually avoided as a precaution, and a staff member with no such concern is the safer choice.
perOption.b: Documented immunity protects the nurse from infection, which makes this the safest assignment.
perOption.c: High-dose steroids weaken the immune system, raising the risk of severe varicella.
perOption.d: Without proven immunity the nurse can still be infected despite a respirator.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Make safe assignments for a client with varicella.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3. Which measures should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clean the hands before every contact with the client
Check the temperature at least every 4 hours and report 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher
Place a vase of fresh flowers from the family in the room to lift the client's mood
Take rectal temperatures for accuracy
Keep a dedicated stethoscope and thermometer in the client's room
Restrict visitors who have colds or other infections

rationale.correct: Neutropenic precautions: strict hand hygiene, temperature monitoring, dedicated equipment, no fresh flowers, no rectal routes, no sick visitors.

perOption.a: Hand hygiene is the most effective way to prevent infection in neutropenia.
perOption.b: Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are too low to cause pus or redness.
perOption.c: Fresh flowers and standing water can carry bacteria and fungi.
perOption.d: Rectal routes can injure the mucosa and introduce bacteria.
perOption.e: Dedicated equipment lowers the risk of carrying organisms from other clients.
perOption.f: Sick visitors can pass infections to a client who cannot fight them.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: After giving a subcutaneous enoxaparin injection, the nurse is stuck in the finger with the used needle. The client has hepatitis C. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wash the puncture site with soap and water right away
Report the exposure to the employee health department or supervisor
Squeeze the finger to make it bleed and apply an alcohol pad to the site
Ask the client to agree to new blood tests for hepatitis and HIV at once

rationale.correct: After a needlestick: wash with soap and water, report at once, and follow the facility's exposure process for testing and follow-up.

perOption.a: Immediate cleaning of the wound is the first step after a needlestick exposure.
perOption.b: Reporting must happen promptly so testing and follow-up can start, but cleaning the wound comes first.
perOption.c: Squeezing the wound and putting caustic agents on it are not recommended.
perOption.d: Source testing is arranged through the facility's process after first aid and reporting.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The home health nurse visits a client with COPD who uses oxygen at 2 L/min through a concentrator. Which finding requires the nurse to teach the client again?

options.text: The oxygen tubing is 15 m (50 ft) long so the client can reach the kitchen
The client lights the gas stove to cook dinner while wearing the nasal cannula
A "No smoking: oxygen in use" sign is posted on the front door of the house
The concentrator is kept in an open area away from curtains and the walls

rationale.correct: Oxygen supports combustion: no smoking, candles or open flames near oxygen, and keep equipment ventilated.

perOption.a: Long tubing is acceptable if it is kept out of walkways; it is not the main hazard.
perOption.b: Open flames near oxygen can cause fire; the client must stay at least 2 m (6 to 10 ft) from flames.
perOption.c: Posting a sign is recommended to warn visitors.
perOption.d: Keeping the concentrator ventilated and clear is correct.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse in a primary care clinic is reviewing immunizations for four clients. Which client should NOT receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine today?

options.text: A 1-year-old child with a mild cold and a temperature of 37.6 °C (99.7 °F)
A postpartum client who is breastfeeding and is not immune to rubella
A client who is 10 weeks pregnant and has a negative rubella titer
A 4-year-old child whose sibling at home is receiving chemotherapy for leukemia

rationale.correct: Live vaccines such as MMR and varicella are contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression; mild illness is not a contraindication.

perOption.a: A mild illness with low-grade fever is not a reason to delay vaccines.
perOption.b: MMR is recommended after birth for non-immune clients and is safe during breastfeeding.
perOption.c: MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy; it is given after birth instead.
perOption.d: Household contacts of immunocompromised people should receive MMR, because the vaccine virus is not spread.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications to the MMR vaccine.

questions.stem: During a well-child visit, the nurse assesses an 18-month-old child. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider for further developmental evaluation?

options.text: The child says about 10 single words and points to things wanted
The child walks well but falls often when trying to run across the room
The child does not look when a parent points to a toy across the room
The child scribbles with a crayon but cannot copy a circle shown by the nurse

rationale.correct: Lack of joint attention, such as not following a point, by 18 months is a red flag for autism spectrum disorder.

perOption.a: An 18-month-old typically says 10 or more words and points to show wants.
perOption.b: Toddlers at 18 months walk well and are still unsteady when running.
perOption.c: Not following a pointed finger (no joint attention) at 18 months is a red flag for autism and needs evaluation.
perOption.d: Copying a circle is expected around age 3; scribbling is normal at 18 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a developmental red flag in a toddler.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is 24 weeks pregnant about warning signs to report right away. Which signs should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: A severe headache that does not go away with acetaminophen
Fluid leaking or gushing from the vagina
Mild swelling of the ankles at the end of the day
Seeing spots or flashing lights
Heartburn after large meals
Fewer fetal movements than usual
Regular tightening of the abdomen 4 or more times in an hour

rationale.correct: Teach clients to report headache, visual changes, fluid leaking, reduced fetal movement, bleeding and regular contractions.

perOption.a: A persistent severe headache can be a sign of preeclampsia.
perOption.b: This may mean the membranes have ruptured early.
perOption.c: Dependent ankle swelling that improves with rest is common in pregnancy.
perOption.d: Visual changes can be a sign of severe preeclampsia.
perOption.e: Heartburn is a common discomfort of pregnancy.
perOption.f: A drop in fetal movement can mean fetal compromise.
perOption.g: Regular contractions before 37 weeks may be preterm labor.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing discharge teaching with a client who gave birth vaginally 2 days ago. Which statement shows the client needs more teaching?

options.text: "If I soak a pad in an hour or pass clots bigger than a golf ball, I'll call right away."
"I can stop taking my prenatal vitamins now, since the baby is here and I feel fine."
"I'll call if I have pain, redness or warmth in one calf."
"My bleeding should change from red to pink to a whitish color over a few weeks."

rationale.correct: Postpartum clients usually continue prenatal vitamins and must know the signs of hemorrhage, infection and thrombosis.

perOption.a: This correctly describes heavy bleeding that needs prompt care.
perOption.b: Prenatal vitamins are usually continued after birth, especially while breastfeeding, so this needs correcting.
perOption.c: These are signs of a deep vein thrombosis, which is a postpartum risk.
perOption.d: This correctly describes the normal progression of lochia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client with no family history of cancer and no symptoms asks the nurse when to start colorectal cancer screening. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Screening begins at 50 for people without a family history, so you have a few years."
"Screening is recommended starting at 45 for adults at average risk, so now is the time."
"Screening is needed only if you notice blood in your stool or a change in bowel habits."
"A yearly digital rectal exam by your provider is enough screening for colon cancer."

rationale.correct: Average-risk adults begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45 with stool-based tests or visual exams such as colonoscopy.

perOption.a: The recommended starting age for average-risk adults was lowered to 45.
perOption.b: Current guidance recommends colorectal cancer screening for average-risk adults from age 45.
perOption.c: Screening is for people without symptoms; symptoms need diagnostic testing.
perOption.d: A digital rectal exam is not a recommended colorectal cancer screening test.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Before discharge, the nurse watches a parent place their newborn in a rear-facing car seat. Which observation shows the car seat is used correctly?

options.text: The harness chest clip sits level with the newborn's armpits
A thick, padded snowsuit is worn under the harness straps
The seat is placed in the front seat so the parent can see the baby
The straps are loose enough to fit two fingers at the collarbone

rationale.correct: Rear-facing in the back seat, snug straps, chest clip at armpit level and no bulky clothing under the harness.

perOption.a: The chest clip belongs at armpit level to keep the straps on the shoulders.
perOption.b: Bulky clothing makes the harness loose in a crash; blankets go over the buckled harness.
perOption.c: Rear-facing seats must not go in front of an active airbag; the back seat is safest.
perOption.d: Straps should be snug: no slack should be pinched at the collarbone.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old client who walks daily and has well-controlled hypertension comes for an annual wellness visit. The client has never had a pneumococcal vaccine. Which recommendation should the nurse expect to discuss?

options.text: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine now, as recommended for all adults 65 and older
Pneumococcal vaccine only if the client develops a chronic lung disease in the future
A yearly pneumococcal booster each fall, given along with the flu vaccine
No pneumococcal vaccine, because the client is active and has no lung disease

rationale.correct: All adults 65 and older are advised to receive pneumococcal vaccination, along with yearly influenza vaccine and other age-based vaccines.

perOption.a: Adults 65 and older who have not had a pneumococcal vaccine are advised to receive a conjugate vaccine.
perOption.b: Age 65 alone is an indication; lung disease is not required.
perOption.c: Pneumococcal vaccine is not given every year.
perOption.d: Good health does not remove the age-based recommendation.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
CDC/ACIP immunization schedules

questions.stem: A 32-year-old client who smokes a pack of cigarettes a day and has migraine with aura asks about birth control. Complete the sentence about the nurse's teaching.

content.template: Because of the client's history, the nurse explains that {{b1}} are not recommended because they increase the risk of {{b2}}, and that {{b3}} is a safe, highly effective option.

options.text: combined estrogen-progestin pills
progestin-only pills
copper intrauterine devices
stroke and blood clots
weight gain and acne
ovarian cysts
a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
the combined vaginal ring
the contraceptive patch

rationale.correct: Migraine with aura and smoking make estrogen-containing methods unsafe; progestin-only or non-hormonal methods are preferred.

perOption.b1:a: Estrogen-containing methods raise clotting and stroke risk in smokers over 35 and in migraine with aura.
perOption.b1:b: Progestin-only methods do not carry the same estrogen-related stroke risk.
perOption.b1:c: The copper IUD contains no hormones and is safe here.
perOption.b2:a: Estrogen with smoking and migraine with aura raises the risk of stroke and venous thrombosis.
perOption.b2:b: These are minor side effects, not the reason to avoid estrogen.
perOption.b2:c: Ovarian cysts are not the main concern with combined pills.
perOption.b3:a: A hormonal IUD is long-acting, highly effective and contains no estrogen.
perOption.b3:b: The ring contains estrogen, so it carries the same risk.
perOption.b3:c: The patch contains estrogen and delivers higher estrogen levels than pills.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old comes to the school clinic alone for a sports physical. During the visit, the teen asks the nurse about sexually transmitted infection testing and asks that parents not be told. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that testing for minors needs a parent's consent, then offer to help the teen talk with them
Tell the teen that STI testing can be done confidentially and arrange the test
Ask the teen to come back for testing with a parent when they are ready to talk about it
Call the parents to discuss the request, since the teen is under 18 and at risk of harm

rationale.correct: Adolescents can consent to confidential STI testing and treatment; nurses protect that confidentiality unless there is a risk of serious harm.

perOption.a: In all U.S. states, minors can consent to STI testing and treatment without a parent.
perOption.b: Minors may consent to STI services confidentially; providing them supports the teen's health.
perOption.c: Delaying testing may cause untreated infection and loses the teen's trust.
perOption.d: Breaking confidentiality for routine STI care is not justified and discourages teens from seeking care.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Provide confidential sexual health care to adolescents.

questions.stem: A client who had a below-the-knee amputation 3 days ago says, "I don't know why they bothered saving me. I'm useless now." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You're not useless. Many people with amputations live full, active lives."
"You're feeling that you have lost your worth since the surgery. Tell me more."
"Would you like me to call the prosthetist so you can see what's available?"
"Why do you think the surgical team should not have saved your life?"

rationale.correct: Reflect feelings and invite the client to say more; avoid false reassurance, advice and "why" questions.

perOption.a: Reassurance dismisses the feelings and closes the conversation.
perOption.b: Reflecting the feeling and inviting more shows empathy and opens the conversation, which also lets the nurse assess for hopelessness.
perOption.c: Problem-solving moves past the client's feelings too quickly.
perOption.d: "Why" questions can make clients defensive.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond therapeutically to a client's loss.

questions.stem: A client admitted for major depressive disorder 5 days ago has been withdrawn and tearful. Today the client is smiling, gives a favorite watch to a roommate and says, "Everything is finally clear to me." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the treatment team that the antidepressant appears to be working
Ask the client directly whether they are thinking about suicide
Encourage the client to join the group activities now that their energy is better
Document the improvement and plan to discuss discharge with the client tomorrow

rationale.correct: Sudden improvement, giving away belongings and statements of resolution can mean a decision to die. Ask directly about suicide and keep the client safe.

perOption.a: A sudden lift in mood with giving away belongings is a warning sign, not proof of recovery.
perOption.b: A sudden calm, giving away possessions and a sense of resolution suggest the client may have made a suicide plan; asking directly is the first step.
perOption.c: More activity is not a priority until suicide risk is assessed.
perOption.d: Discharge planning would miss a possible imminent suicide risk.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client comes to the emergency department after a house fire destroyed their home last night. The client is crying, pacing and says they cannot think. For each category, select the nurse's appropriate actions.

options.text: Stay with the client and speak in short, calm sentences
Explore the client's childhood experiences with loss
Move the client to a quieter area away from the waiting room
Help the client identify a place to stay tonight
Tell the client that things happen for a reason
Connect the client with a disaster relief agency

rationale.correct: Crisis intervention is short and focused: safety, calm presence, fewer stimuli, immediate needs and links to resources.

perOption.a: Presence and simple communication lower anxiety in crisis.
perOption.b: Long-term therapy topics do not belong in the acute crisis.
perOption.c: Fewer stimuli help a client in severe anxiety focus.
perOption.d: Crisis intervention addresses immediate needs such as shelter.
perOption.e: This is a cliché that dismisses the client's feelings.
perOption.f: Linking to resources supports the client's coping after the visit.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan crisis intervention after a disaster.

questions.stem: A client whose spouse died 14 months ago tells the nurse they still set the spouse's place at the table, have not left the house except for groceries and cannot stop thinking about the death. What should the nurse recognize about these findings?

options.text: They are a normal part of grief in the first two years after a loss
They suggest prolonged grief disorder, which needs referral for treatment
They are best explained by an anxiety disorder that began after the death
They show the denial stage of grief, which should resolve on its own

rationale.correct: Grief that stays intense and disabling more than 12 months after a death may be prolonged grief disorder and needs referral.

perOption.a: Grief often lasts many months, but daily intense longing with withdrawal that disrupts life after more than a year is not typical.
perOption.b: Intense longing and preoccupation that disrupt daily life more than 12 months after a death meet the picture of prolonged grief disorder.
perOption.c: The symptoms center on the lost person rather than on general worry or fear.
perOption.d: Setting a place is not denial of the death, and waiting delays needed care.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish prolonged grief disorder from normal grief.

questions.stem: A client with opioid use disorder was admitted 30 hours ago for cellulitis of the forearm and last used heroin just before admission. The client is restless and asks for "something to take the edge off." Highlight the findings that indicate opioid withdrawal.

rationale.correct: Opioid withdrawal causes dilated pupils, rhinorrhea, tearing, gooseflesh, yawning, cramps and diarrhea; it is very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening.

perOption.r1: Pupil dilation is a sign of opioid withdrawal; intoxication causes pinpoint pupils.
perOption.r2: Rhinorrhea and lacrimation are classic withdrawal signs.
perOption.r4: Normal; opioid intoxication would slow breathing.
perOption.r5: Gastrointestinal upset is common in withdrawal.
perOption.r6: Withdrawal does not usually change orientation, unlike alcohol withdrawal delirium.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old client with anorexia nervosa weighs 38 kg (BMI 14.2) and started nutritional rehabilitation 3 days ago. Today the client reports weakness and shortness of breath. Heart rate is 118/min with new irregular beats, ankles are swollen, and labs show phosphorus 1.4 mg/dL, potassium 2.9 mEq/L and magnesium 1.3 mg/dL. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Acute heart failure from viral myocarditis

actions.text: Notify the provider so the calorie intake can be reduced and advanced more slowly
Encourage the client to finish every meal to restore weight faster
Give an extra liter of IV fluid to treat the tachycardia
Allow the client to exercise in the room to build strength

parameters.text: Serum phosphorus, potassium and magnesium levels
Body weight checked once a week
Calories eaten at each meal compared with the meal plan

rationale.correct: Refeeding syndrome is a shift of phosphorus, potassium and magnesium into cells when nutrition restarts; it is treated by slowing feeding, replacing electrolytes and monitoring the heart.

perOption.c1: Low phosphorus, potassium and magnesium with heart and fluid changes days after refeeding starts is refeeding syndrome.
perOption.c2: Edema and tachycardia fit, but the timing with refeeding and the electrolyte pattern point to refeeding syndrome.
perOption.c3: Nothing suggests high glucose or ketoacids.
perOption.c4: There is no fever or other sign of hypermetabolism.
perOption.a1: Slowing the feeding plan reduces the shifts of electrolytes into cells.
perOption.a2: Low potassium, magnesium and phosphorus can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
perOption.a4: The client already shows fluid overload; extra fluid can cause heart failure.
perOption.a5: Exercise raises energy demand and cardiac strain in an unstable client.
perOption.p1: Electrolytes guide replacement and show whether the syndrome is improving.
perOption.p2: Dysrhythmias are the main danger of refeeding syndrome.
perOption.p3: Weekly weights are too infrequent to detect fluid shifts; daily weights are used.
perOption.p4: Intake is tracked, but it does not show whether the dangerous complications are resolving.
perOption.p5: Important for the eating disorder, but not the parameters that show physiologic response.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client with mild Alzheimer's disease is admitted for a hip fracture. On the second night the client pulls at the IV, does not know where they are and sees "bugs on the wall." The family says the client was calm and oriented to home and family before admission. What do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Progression of Alzheimer's disease to a more severe stage
Delirium, an acute change that needs a search for its cause
Sundowning, which is expected in dementia and needs no treatment
A new psychotic disorder that needs an antipsychotic drug started

rationale.correct: A sudden change in attention and awareness, often with hallucinations, is delirium until proven otherwise, even in a client with dementia.

perOption.a: Dementia worsens over months to years, not over one night.
perOption.b: A sudden change with hallucinations and inattention is delirium, which has a treatable cause such as pain, infection, drugs or hypoxia.
perOption.c: Sundowning can occur, but new hallucinations and a sharp change from baseline point to delirium.
perOption.d: New psychosis at 84 with an acute medical problem is most likely delirium.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
